User Guide

Start with Construct values if you are preparing inputs. This guide moves from operations on one value to elementwise operations on vectors and functions of whole matrices.

Scalar calculations

Use ordinary Julia arithmetic and functions with the extended types. Scalar operations summarizes available operations and Special Functions covers Bessel, gamma, and other functions.

using DoubleFloats

x = df64"1e-20"
println("log1p(x) = ", string(log1p(x)))
println("expm1(x) = ", string(expm1(x)))
log1p(x) = 9.999999999999999999949999999999986e-21
expm1(x) = 1.0000000000000000000049999999999863e-20

Use log1p(x) for log(1 + x) and expm1(x) for exp(x) - 1 when x is small. These scalar functions avoid rounding away the small difference in the intermediate result. For a worked validation, see Choosing and checking precision.

For Double64, exp overflows near an input of 709.78 and rounds to zero near −745.13. The exponential kernels account for subnormal rounding. Near a rounding midpoint they may use a higher-precision fallback. A Double32 result can have a subnormal low component even when its high component is normal. The Accuracy Report shows when this absolute rounding step dominates the relative working-precision score. See the Technical Guide for details and the Benchmark Report for timings.

The faster Double64 and Double32 paths apply automatically in their input ranges. Small Double64 sinh and tanh arguments use direct approximations. Ordinary Double32 arguments can use a single Float64 evaluation when it retains the input's low component. See the technical sections on Double64 and Double32 for the ranges and how these paths handle sensitive inputs.

Elementwise operations on vectors

Ordinary Julia broadcasting applies a scalar function to each element. Use y = sin.(x) to allocate a result, or y .= sin.(x) to write into an existing array. For vector batches try DoubleFloats.simdmap!, which reuses a destination and can use specialized kernels. It returns the destination.

Evaluate a batch of angles

The broadcast version produces one tuple per angle. The batch version writes those tuples into a reusable vector. The grid uses exactly representable binary fractions at its endpoints.

using DoubleFloats

angles = Double64.(range(0.25, 2; length=4096))
reference = sincos.(angles)

pairs = Vector{Tuple{Double64,Double64}}(undef, length(angles))
DoubleFloats.simdmap!(sincos, pairs, angles)

max_error = maximum(zip(pairs, reference)) do (got, want)
    max(abs(got[1] - want[1]), abs(got[2] - want[2]))
end

@assert max_error < df64"1e-29"
println("Processed ", length(angles), " angles")
Processed 4096 angles

Inputs, outputs, and execution order

The batch API takes one or two input vectors. Power also accepts a single scalar exponent for the whole batch. With angles and pairs from above, related calls include these.

values = similar(angles)
other = reverse(angles)

DoubleFloats.simdmap!(^, values, angles, 5)
DoubleFloats.simdmap!(atan, values, angles, other)
DoubleFloats.simdmap!(hypot, values, angles, other)
DoubleFloats.simdmap!(DoubleFloats.normalize, pairs, angles, other)
nothing

Every vector must have the same axes (valid indices) as the destination. A mismatch throws DimensionMismatch before any writes. The operation uses elementwise indexing without broadcast expansion. Paired normalization stores one (x/h, z/h) tuple per element for ordinary finite inputs, using the pair's hypotenuse h. Assignment uses the destination's usual conversion rules. For example, a cis call on a real NaN produces a real NaN, which is then converted if the destination holds complex values. Overlapping inputs, including exact in-place and shifted overlaps, are read from their values at entry. Snapshots can allocate. Custom vector storage also uses snapshots when overlap cannot be ruled out.

By default the operation is serial. If a scalar call or assignment throws, earlier elements have been written and later elements keep their original values. Dense, disjoint Double64, ComplexDF64, and Double32 vectors can use SIMD for supported operations and input ranges. For example, dense Double32 input with angles between 0.125 and 0.5 radians can use a native tan kernel.

angles32 = Double32.(range(0.125, 0.5; length=4096))
tangents = DoubleFloats.simdmap!(tan, similar(angles32), angles32)

Views, other precisions, unsupported result types, and out-of-range blocks use scalar methods. A native kernel can round differently from the scalar call because it uses a different evaluation formula.

Pass threaded=true to allow eligible operations to run on multiple Julia threads. Run Julia with multiple threads, for example julia -t 4. Threading requires sufficiently long, disjoint dense vectors and works for many functions that use scalar arithmetic internally. Custom callables still run in index order. If a worker fails, the call can raise a task exception after other chunks have written to the destination. Keep the default when the order of writes on failure matters.

See the Technical Guide for SIMD coverage and measured performance.

Work with matrices

Load LinearAlgebra for standard operations such as norm, eigen, and matrix factorizations. Use A \ b to solve a system and A * B for matrix multiplication.

A dot changes the operation. exp.(A) applies the scalar exponential to each entry, while exp(A) computes the exponential of the matrix using matrix algebra. For example, exp.(A) replaces every zero entry with one, while the matrix exponential of a triangular matrix retains its triangular structure. See Linear Algebra for a worked example and the supported function families.
